# Routing

*15 of 31 rules below are **designed** rather than shipped, and are marked where they appear.*

<a id="routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered"></a>

## A route is a `#[Route]` compiled into the unit's table, its three runtime bugs are compile errors, and one method's routes share one path  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`

A route is declared where its handler is: `#[Route(path: "/users/{id}", method: Http\Method::Get)]`
on a method, and the method is the route's identity. The compiler reads every such attribute, through the program
enumeration [`programs/implementing`](programs.md#programs-implementing) already built, into a route table baked into the compiled
unit. Nothing registers a route at run time — there is no routes file, no `$router->get(...)`, and no
generated cache to warm or go stale, because the work that cache exists to save is done while compiling.

Three bugs every runtime router discovers late are compile errors here, each naming both sites. **Two
routes claiming the same verb and the same path shape** — `/users/{id}` and `/users/{userId}` are one
shape, and a capture's type never disambiguates two declarations, because a rule under which it did
would make matching depend on declaration order after all. **A `{name}` capture with no parameter of
that name** on the annotated method. **A link to a method that has no route**
([`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked)).

**Several `#[Route]`s on one method share one `path` and differ by verb**, which is how one method
serves several verbs. Two different paths on one method do not compile, naming both attributes, and
the message suggests an optional segment `{x?}` ([`routing/a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent`](routing.md#routing-a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent)) or a
second method. One path per method is what keeps a link a function of its method: `url()` has one
answer and no rule to choose between two declarations. Two attributes sharing both `path` and
`method` remain the duplicate-route error however they are grouped.

The limit is the one the design buys. A route cannot be added at run time, so a CMS with
database-defined URLs matches its own way and uses none of this — and because the router stops at
matching ([`routing/matching-is-not-dispatching`](routing.md#routing-matching-is-not-dispatching)), using none of it, half of it, or `url` alone
costs nothing.

**Declined:**
- **A runtime registry** (`$router->get("/users/{id}", …)`). It moves all three checks to run time,
  needs a generated cache file to be fast, and makes registration order part of what a route means.
- **A route table in `nvs.toml`.** A URL is source state: the code that handles a path and the path
  itself change together, in the same commit. A schedule is deployment state, which is why it is
  the opposite case ([`config/scheduled-work-is-a-config-block`](config.md#config-scheduled-work-is-a-config-block)).
- **Building the table from a `Core\Ast` walk at run time**
  ([`tooling/reflection-and-source-parsing-are-core-features`](tooling.md#tooling-reflection-and-source-parsing-are-core-features)). It parses the program again
  inside a request, gets none of the three compile-time checks, and puts the parser on the request
  path for something the compiler already knows.
- **Two paths on one method, with `url()` taking a verb to choose between them.** Callers would pass
  an argument for one route's shape and not another's, and `url()` would need a rule to choose between
  two declarations.
- **Captures' types disambiguating two routes at the same path**, `/{id}` on `uint` beside `/{slug}`
  on `string`. It brings order-dependence back and makes the duplicate check partial rather than
  total.

<sub>See also [`routing/table-is-opt-in`](routing.md#routing-table-is-opt-in), [`routing/matching-is-not-dispatching`](routing.md#routing-matching-is-not-dispatching), [`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked), [`programs/implementing`](programs.md#programs-implementing), [`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute), [`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type).</sub>

<a id="routing-route-attribute"></a>

## `#[Route]` is `{path, method, slotted?}` on a method, recognized by name and never by shape, and the method is the route's identity  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/route-attribute`

`type Core\Route = {path: string, method: Core\Http\Method, slotted?: bool};` — an ordinary
[`attributes/inert-metadata`](attributes.md#attributes-inert-metadata) alias, attached the ordinary way, with one difference: the compiler
acts on it only when the name **resolves** to `Core\Route`. It sits on
[`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute)'s closed list of compiler-recognized attributes and is matched
nominally, so a userland `type Route = {...};` and a framework's own `Route`-shaped anonymous object declare
no route however they are spelled.

- **`method` is an enum case**, the same `Core\Http\Method` that `Core\Request::method` answers,
  never a string ([`attributes/payload-is-a-compile-time-constant`](attributes.md#attributes-payload-is-a-compile-time-constant)). `path` and `method` are
  required; an attribute naming neither declares nothing and is refused.
- **The attribute is repeatable** ([`attributes/repeatable`](attributes.md#attributes-repeatable)), which is how one method serves two
  verbs. There is no `methods:` list and no wildcard verb. Every `#[Route]` on one method writes the
  same `path` ([`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered)).
- **Methods only**, `static` or instance, and the method may take parameters the path does not name
  — a `Request`, a service — which the router ignores.
- **A route is identified by its method.** There is no `name` field: a link, a match check, a signed
  link and the API document all name the route with a method reference such as `Shop::show`
  ([`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked)), so every route is linkable.
- **`slotted` is optional and `false` when absent.** It is the route half of
  [`core-classes/html-later`](core-classes.md#core-classes-html-later)'s slotted delivery, and the route table carries it.

A `#[Route]` method also carries an `#[Access]` ([`attributes/access-is-a-required-sibling`](attributes.md#attributes-access-is-a-required-sibling)).

The closed list only works if every entry on it is argued: a compiler-recognized attribute that is
cheap to add is how an attribute set becomes an undocumented second language surface.

**Declined:**
- **Structural matching**, the way [`attributes/structural-retrieval`](attributes.md#attributes-structural-retrieval) retrieves an attribute. A
  framework's own `Route`-shaped literal would register routes Novis does not own
  ([`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute)).
- **A `name` field.** It is a second identity beside the method, with a mapping to learn and a
  duplicate-name error to keep. A link written by name is a string the editor cannot follow, while a
  method reference is checked while compiling and followed like any other. A method rename changes
  every reference with it, so the rename that a name existed to survive is a refactor, not a break.
- **A class-level prefix attribute** (`#[Route(path: "/admin")]` on a class). It interacts badly
  with inheritance and hides a route's real path from the line that declares it; a prefix is a
  framework opinion.
- **A `host` field.** A hostname in the compiled table would end the relocatability mounts buy
  ([`routing/a-request-reads-its-mount`](routing.md#routing-a-request-reads-its-mount)), and the duplicate-route compile error would grow a host
  dimension.

<sub>See also [`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute), [`attributes/inert-metadata`](attributes.md#attributes-inert-metadata), [`attributes/repeatable`](attributes.md#attributes-repeatable), [`attributes/payload-is-a-compile-time-constant`](attributes.md#attributes-payload-is-a-compile-time-constant), [`attributes/access-is-a-required-sibling`](attributes.md#attributes-access-is-a-required-sibling), [`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered), [`routing/no-wildcard-verb`](routing.md#routing-no-wildcard-verb).</sub>

<a id="routing-path-grammar"></a>

## A path is fixed segments and three capture forms, each capture a whole segment naming a parameter

`rule:routing/path-grammar`

A path is a string literal beginning at the root, validated while checking, whose segments are
fixed segments or captures:

- **`{name}`** captures one whole segment.
- **`{name?}`** captures one whole segment **or none**. Last position only, at most once, never in
  the same path as a `{name...}`, and the parameter it binds must have a default — that is what makes
  the absent case well-typed rather than nullable by accident; a `{name?}` bound to a parameter
  without one is a compile error naming both. `/posts/` does not match `/posts/{page?}`: an empty
  final segment is not an absent one ([`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused)).
- **`{name...}`** captures every remaining segment as one `tainted string`, last position only.
- Everything else is a fixed segment, compared byte for byte and case-sensitively
  ([`classes/names-resolve-case-sensitively`](classes.md#classes-names-resolve-case-sensitively)).

A capture is a whole segment: `/u{id}` and `/{id}.json` are refused, not partially matched. Every
capture names a parameter of the method it is attached to, and that parameter's type is what the
segment converts to ([`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type)).

**Declined:**
- **`:name` placeholders.** `:` is a legal character inside a path segment (`/a:b` is a valid path),
  so `:name` would need an escape rule the braced form does not; and the braced form is what
  OpenAPI, Laravel, Symfony, axum and ASP.NET all use, so it is the spelling a reader arrives with.
- **An inline constraint** (`{id:uint}`). The type is already written on the parameter, and a
  constraint stated in two places is one that can disagree; a closed set is a literal-union type on
  the parameter ([`routing/a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set`](routing.md#routing-a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set)).

<sub>See also [`routing/precedence-is-structural`](routing.md#routing-precedence-is-structural), [`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type), [`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused), [`classes/names-resolve-case-sensitively`](classes.md#classes-names-resolve-case-sensitively), [`routing/a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent`](routing.md#routing-a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent).</sub>

<a id="routing-no-wildcard-verb"></a>

## There is no wildcard verb: `method` is required, singular, and one case of a closed enum

`rule:routing/no-wildcard-verb`

There is no `Method::Any`, no omitted `method` and no multi-valued `method`. `method` is required,
singular, and one case of the closed enum `Core\Http\Method`; a `#[Route]` written without one is
`E0747`. This is a decision, not a deferral, because two mechanisms read the exact verb set a
wildcard would erase:

- **`Core\Router::methodsFor`** answers the verbs a path serves — an empty list is a `404`, a
  non-empty one is a `405` with an `Allow:` header naming them. A wildcard makes that header either
  unanswerable or a dump of the whole enum, and `405` stops being reachable.
- **CSRF is classified per verb** ([`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default)) — on for `POST`, `PUT`,
  `PATCH` and `DELETE`, off for the safe verbs — from the declaration, not from the request. A
  wildcard declares a route that is half unsafe.

A wildcard could not even mean *any* verb honestly: `Core\Http\Method` is closed
([`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type)), so it would mean the cases this version of `Core` happens to
name, silently changing meaning when one is added.

[`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered) gives the ergonomics a wildcard
was wanted for — one method, one `url()` target, one metrics series. What it does not give is one
*line*, and that is the point: each verb a route answers stays visible at the declaration, where
`methodsFor` and the CSRF classification read it. A method serving a safe and an unsafe verb carries
one `#[Access]` for both, and the CSRF check is still per verb from that one declaration.

**Declined:**
- **A `methods: array<Method>` field on the attribute.** It gives one route two syntaxes and makes the
  repeatable attribute redundant ([`routing/route-attribute`](routing.md#routing-route-attribute)).

<sub>See also [`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered), [`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default), [`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type), [`routing/a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path`](routing.md#routing-a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path).</sub>

<a id="routing-precedence-is-structural"></a>

## Precedence is structural — a fixed segment beats a capture beats an optional beats a catch-all — never declaration order

`rule:routing/precedence-is-structural`

Where two routes of one verb both match a path, the one with more fixed segments wins, segment by
segment: a fixed segment beats a `{name}`, which beats a `{name?}`, which beats a `{name...}`. `/users/new` and
`/users/{id}` coexist with no ordering rule to remember, and moving a declaration between files
cannot change which route answers. That is what makes the table order-independent at all, and it is
why two routes with the same verb and the same shape are refused rather than ordered
([`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered)).

A failed conversion is not a match: `/users/abc` against `show(uint $id)` passes on to the next
candidate, and is a `404` only if nothing else claims the path
([`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type)). A `{name?}` is one node marked terminal, so
`/posts` and `/posts/2` each cost one walk rather than two.

The model is the radix-trie rule `matchit` implements — the rule is the precedence, not the data
structure, and a matcher is free to compute the same answer by ranking rows.

**Declined:**
- **Declaration-order precedence**, first match wins, which is what a linear route list gives. Moving
  a declaration between files becomes a behaviour change, and a routing file has to be read top to
  bottom to be understood.

<sub>See also [`routing/path-grammar`](routing.md#routing-path-grammar), [`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered), [`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set"></a>

## A capture narrows to a closed set with a set of allowed values or an enum-subset type, never with a regex

`rule:routing/a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set`

A capture's type may be a **set of allowed `string` or `int` values**, or a **subset of an enum's
cases** ([`types/single-value-types`](types.md#types-single-value-types)), beside the scalar and enum types a capture already converts to.
`show("en"|"de"|"fr" $lang)` narrows the segment to a closed set with no grammar of its own: `/fr/docs/intro`
matches, `/xx/docs/intro` does not and falls through to a `404` by the failed-conversion rule
([`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type)) rather than reaching the handler. The narrowing
is a property of the table, not a check the handler was trusted to write, and the generated API document
emits the set as `enum: [en, de, fr]`.

The constraint is written where the type is written. The inline `{id:uint}` grammar room is deliberately
not taken — the same fact in two places that can disagree — and **a regex constraint is refused
outright, as a security decision**: an application-authored pattern over the request path runs before
any rate limiting, so catastrophic backtracking is a denial of service open to any unauthenticated
client, so security decides it and simplicity agrees ([`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority)). A shape a type
cannot express — a `[a-z0-9-]+` slug — stays a `Core\Validate` check inside the handler, answering `400`.

`Core\Router::url` builds a link for every member of the set and refuses a value written outside it at
compile time; a computed value is substituted and encoded. Which text an enum case is spelled by — in
a segment, in a link and in the generated document alike — is
[`routing/an-enum-capture-is-spelled-by-its-backing-value-or-its-case-name`](routing.md#routing-an-enum-capture-is-spelled-by-its-backing-value-or-its-case-name).

<sub>See also [`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type), [`types/single-value-types`](types.md#types-single-value-types), [`core-classes/validate-has-no-type-predicates`](core-classes.md#core-classes-validate-has-no-type-predicates), [`programs/memory-priority`](programs.md#programs-memory-priority), [`routing/a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string`](routing.md#routing-a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string), [`routing/path-grammar`](routing.md#routing-path-grammar), [`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table).</sub>

<a id="routing-an-enum-capture-is-spelled-by-its-backing-value-or-its-case-name"></a>

## An enum capture is spelled by a written backing value, and by its case name when the value was counted

`rule:routing/an-enum-capture-is-spelled-by-its-backing-value-or-its-case-name`

An enum capture matches on its case's **written** backing value, and on the **case name** when the
value was counted rather than written, in a path segment and in a `#[Query]` value alike.

Every Novis enum is backed by one integer type and nothing else ([`enums/one-backing-type`](enums.md#enums-one-backing-type)), so
there is no backed-versus-pure split to inherit; what decides the spelling is whether the integer was
written in the enum body:

- Every admitted case's value written — the segment is that integer, parsed as the enum's backing
  type.
- Any admitted case's value counted on from the one before it ([`enums/declaration`](enums.md#enums-declaration)) — the whole
  subset is spelled by case name, compared byte for byte and case-sensitively, as a fixed segment
  is ([`classes/names-resolve-case-sensitively`](classes.md#classes-names-resolve-case-sensitively)).

The choice is per subset and never per case, because a subset mixing the two would put an integer and
a name in the same position, and a case may legally be named `7`.

A counted value is not an identifier: `enum Status { Active, Banned }` gives `Active` the value `0`
only because it is written first, so inserting a case ahead of it would repoint `/0` at a different
case and silently change what every link already in the world means. A written value is one its
author stated and intends to keep, which is why it is the one that reaches the URL.

Two cases may carry the same value ([`enums/declaration`](enums.md#enums-declaration)), and a subset admitting two of them
under the written-value spelling is a **compile error** naming both cases and the value, rather than
a silent first-wins ([`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused)). Under the case-name spelling an alias is
fine, because the names are still distinct.

A segment naming no admitted case is not a match and falls through to a `404`
([`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type)), exactly as a failed `int` conversion does.
One spelling serves every position: it is what the match converts, what `Core\Router::url` writes
into a link and refuses outside the set ([`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked)), and what
the generated document lists in `enum: [...]`, so a route, its links and its document cannot
disagree.

The spelling is decided once while compiling (`nvs_types::routes`' `enum_capture`) and every position
reads that one answer: the match converts on it, the link is refused against it and renders through
the spelling rows the prepared template carries, and the document lists it. The one position still
short of it is a `#[Query]` value's **arrival**, and not for a reason of this rule's: no query value
of any declared type is bound to its parameter yet, which is
[`routing/a-bad-query-value-is-a-400`](routing.md#routing-a-bad-query-value-is-a-400)'s own unshipped half.

**Declined:**
- **The case name always.** It makes a written backing value decorative: an author who wrote
  `Active = 1` to pin a public number gets `Active` in the URL anyway, and an identifier from the
  source reaches the URL surface whether or not its author meant it to be public.
- **The backing value always.** Every counted value is then a public identifier that an insertion
  moves.
- **An attribute naming the spelling per enum.** A third place the same fact could be written and
  disagree with the other two, the objection [`routing/path-grammar`](routing.md#routing-path-grammar) makes to `{id:uint}`.

<sub>See also [`routing/a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set`](routing.md#routing-a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set), [`routing/a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture`](routing.md#routing-a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture), [`enums/declaration`](enums.md#enums-declaration), [`enums/one-backing-type`](enums.md#enums-one-backing-type), [`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type), [`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent"></a>

## `{name?}` captures one trailing segment or none, and its parameter's default is what makes the absent case well-typed

`rule:routing/a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent`

`{name?}` captures one whole segment or none. It is permitted only in the last position, at most once,
and never in the same path as a `{name...}`. **The method parameter it binds must have a default** —
that is what makes the absent case well-typed rather than nullable by accident — and a `{name?}` whose
parameter has none is a compile error naming both sites, as is one in any other position.

Precedence slots it below `{name}` and above `{name...}`, so the structural rule extends with no
ordering to remember; in the trie it is one node marked terminal, costing a static hit's walk rather
than a second one. `/posts` matches `/posts/{page?}` with the parameter's default and `/posts/3` with
`3`. **`/posts/` matches neither**: an empty final segment is not an absent one, and repairing the
difference is what [`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused) refuses.

It replaces the two-attribute spelling for one endpoint, which is legal but carries two paths — so the
two forms needed two methods, so one link could not reach both, and metrics saw one endpoint
as two series. A link built with the optional capture left out of `$params` simply drops the segment.

**Declined:**
- **Two paths on one method.** It weakens the one-path-per-method compile error
  ([`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered)) and turns `url()` from a table lookup into a
  best-fit search.

<sub>See also [`routing/a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path`](routing.md#routing-a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path), [`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused), [`routing/path-grammar`](routing.md#routing-path-grammar), [`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture"></a>

## A `#[Query]` parameter is declared with a capture's type list, and a default is what makes it optional

`rule:routing/a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture`

`#[Query]` on a parameter of a `#[Route]` method declares that the parameter is bound from the request's
query string, by the parameter's own name — the attribute carries nothing that could give it another
key. It is one of the compiler-recognised attributes and is matched nominally
([`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute)): a userland `type Query = {...};` binds nothing, and a `#[Query]`
on a method that declares no route is refused rather than ignored.

The parameter takes the same type list as a path capture and launders the same way
([`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type)): `string`, `int`, `uint`, `decimal`,
`Core\Uuid`, an enum, a closed set ([`routing/a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set`](routing.md#routing-a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set)), or a class
implementing `Parses`; anything else is a compile error at the parameter. **A default is what makes the key optional**; a parameter without
one is required. Both facts are what the generated API document reads
([`attributes/api-adds-and-cannot-contradict`](attributes.md#attributes-api-adds-and-cannot-contradict)), and a declared `#[Query]` key is what
`Core\Router::url` accepts beyond the captures ([`routing/a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string`](routing.md#routing-a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string)).

A query value takes no part in choosing a route, so it can never reintroduce the declaration-order
dependence structural precedence exists to prevent — which is what makes the binding safe to add at
all. How a bad value fails is [`routing/a-bad-query-value-is-a-400`](routing.md#routing-a-bad-query-value-is-a-400).

**Declined:**
- **No query binding, and no query parameters in the generated document.** Every endpoint would
  validate its own query by hand, and the document would miss most of its parameters, which is most
  of what a client author reads it for.
- **A `query:` field on `#[Route]`.** It puts a list of bindings away from the parameters it names. A
  sibling attribute is how `#[Route]` is extended, as `#[Access]` already is.

<sub>See also [`routing/a-bad-query-value-is-a-400`](routing.md#routing-a-bad-query-value-is-a-400), [`routing/a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set`](routing.md#routing-a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set), [`routing/a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string`](routing.md#routing-a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string), [`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type), [`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute), [`attributes/api-adds-and-cannot-contradict`](attributes.md#attributes-api-adds-and-cannot-contradict), [`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-bad-query-value-is-a-400"></a>

## A `#[Query]` value that does not convert is a `400`, where a path capture the matcher cannot convert is a `404`

`rule:routing/a-bad-query-value-is-a-400`

A `#[Query]` parameter's value converts to its declared type and arrives unqualified, exactly as a path
capture does, and fails differently. A path capture that the matcher cannot convert means *this route is
not the one*: matching continues, and a miss is a `404`. A query value takes no part in choosing a route,
so there is nothing to continue to: the route matched and the input is bad, which is what `400` means. A
required key that is absent is a `400` for the same reason, and the handler's own body never runs.

**A path capture at a class built from text is on the query value's side of that line**, and for the
query value's reason. That class is not one of the conversions the matcher performs
([`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type)): the matcher matches its segment on shape and
the class converts it where the match crosses into the program, so by the time the class can refuse
anything the route has already been chosen and there is nothing to continue to. Its refusal is therefore
a `400`. What makes the two kinds of capture differ is which of them the router itself reads. Running an
implementor's `parse` in the matcher would put a body that can loop, allocate and throw over every
request URL, including the ones that match nothing.

The divergence is the point rather than an inconsistency, and it is pinned as one: one case asserts a
path capture's `404` and a text-built capture's `400` side by side, so a reader holding two adjacent
lines of one signature knows they fail two ways.

**A key written twice is a `400` too**, for a parameter that takes one value: neither value is picked
([`errors/ambiguous-input-refused`](errors.md#errors-ambiguous-input-refused)). So is a bracketed key such as `page[]=1`, which builds a list.

`Core\Router::dispatch` binds each `#[Query]` parameter when it calls a route method, after the match
and before `allows`. It reads the query string through the parser `Core\Request::query()` uses, once per
request and only for a route that declares a `#[Query]` parameter, so a route without one costs nothing
more. An absent optional key gives the declared default. Every failure above is `refused` with
`BadCapture` and the match.

<sub>See also [`routing/a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture`](routing.md#routing-a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture), [`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-method-is-one-endpoint-everywhere"></a>

## A method is one `url()` target, one `Match::is` for every verb, and one `operationId` per verb  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/a-method-is-one-endpoint-everywhere`

A method whose repeated `#[Route]`s serve several verbs is one endpoint everywhere it is observed:

- **`Core\Router::url(App::receive)` returns the one path**, because every `#[Route]` on one method
  shares its `path` ([`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered)), which makes method-to-path a
  function. No verb argument is added to `url` or `urlAbsolute`; a caller that needs to know which
  verb to send already knows.
- **`Core\Router\Match::is(App::receive)` is `true` for every verb the method serves**, and
  `Match::method()` tells the verbs apart where that matters
  ([`routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`](routing.md#routing-a-match-is-not-invocable)).
- **The generated `operationId` is `Class.method`, with the lowercased verb appended when the method
  serves several verbs** — `App.receive.post`, `App.receive.put`. OpenAPI requires the id to be unique
  per operation, and `(path, method)` is unique by the duplicate-route rule, so the suffix is
  deterministic and needs no counter. A method that serves one verb is emitted bare. `#[Api]`'s
  `operationId` replaces the derived id
  ([`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table)).
- **The metrics `route` label is the one path pattern for every verb**
  ([`observability/route-label-is-the-path-pattern`](observability.md#observability-route-label-is-the-path-pattern)), so a dashboard shows one series per endpoint.

The route table's shape does not change: one row per `(path, method)`, each carrying its handler, and
the reverse index `url()` reads is keyed by the handler. Runtime cost is zero: a written reference
folds to the row index while compiling.

<sub>See also [`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered), [`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table), [`routing/an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin`](routing.md#routing-an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin), [`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked).</sub>

<a id="routing-matching-is-not-dispatching"></a>

## A match is a route identity and typed parameters, and running a handler is a separate call the program makes  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/matching-is-not-dispatching`

```nvs
Core\Request::route(): ?Router\Match;                                   // the match the server made
Core\Router::match(Http\Method $method, tainted string $path): ?Router\Match;
Core\Router::methodsFor(tainted string $path): array<Http\Method>;      // [] ⇒ 404, else 405 + Allow:
Core\Router::url(callable $route, array<string, mixed> $params = []): string;         // launder (URL path)
Core\Router::urlAbsolute(callable $route, array<string, mixed> $params = []): string; // launder (URL)
Core\Router\Match::is(callable $route): bool;                           // did this method's route matchCore\Router\Match::params(): array<tainted string|int|uint|decimal|Core\Uuid|Parses>;
Core\Router\Match::param(string $name): ?(tainted string|int|uint|decimal|Core\Uuid|Parses);
Core\Router\Match::method(): Http\Method;
Core\Router\Match::access(): ?string;                                   // the resolved name of `allow:`
Core\Router\Match::accessAs<E>(): ?E;                                   // `allow:` as a case of enum E
Core\Router\Match::attribute<T>(): ?T;                                  // the method's payload of shape T
```

The server matches a request once, before any application code, and `Core\Request::route()` is that
match; `match` asks the same table about a verb and a path the program chose. Either answers which
method's route matched, through `is`, typed captures, the declared verb and the access decision, and **nothing invocable** — no `->invoke()`,
no callable, no class-and-method strings. Matching and dispatching are two steps: a match is data, and
the one call that runs a handler is `Core\Router::dispatch`, whose jump the compiler generates from
the table and whose gate answers every request the handler does not run for
([`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler)).

A program may also dispatch by hand. Any route in the table may have matched, so a capture's type is
one union and a read is guarded by `is`: one `if` per route, such as
`if ($match->is(Shop::show))`, in which the program states the type a capture already is with `as`.
A reference written at the call folds to the route's row index while compiling, and one passed as a
value is compared by row when the call runs. The same reference reads "is this the current page" in a
template, so a link and a match check name a route the same way. The access decision rides on the match uninterpreted
([`security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`](security.md#security-access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning)), so a hand-written dispatcher checks it
once above those checks and the check covers every arm. `accessAs<E>()` answers it as a case of the
enum `E` the call site writes, and `null` when it is not one of `E`'s cases; `access()` answers the
resolved name of the constant `allow:` wrote, which is the only reading of a class constant.

A program can call `dispatch`, write its own `switch`, use `url` alone, or ignore all of it, and none
of those choices is penalised; keeping the match separate from the call is what makes the table
adoptable piece by piece. Hand-written dispatch costs a list of every route that nothing checks,
which is what `dispatch` removes.

Typed `callable` would not move this line: routes share no signature and handlers no return type, so
routing is not a case that forces [`types/grammar`](types.md#types-grammar)'s deferral. Signing a route's identity is
[`core-classes/router-signed-url`](core-classes.md#core-classes-router-signed-url).

**Declined**, each because it is a framework opinion:
- **An invocable match.** Dispatch is a call the program makes, and the match it reads stays data
  ([`routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`](routing.md#routing-a-match-is-not-invocable)).
- **A controller convention.** No base class, naming rule or directory layout.
- **A built-in return-value-to-response rule.** A returned value reaches the response only through the
  program's own `Core\Router\Responder::respond`, so the program decides what each value sends
  ([`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler)).
- **Middleware, filters, groups or a route-level rate limit.** The gate is the one place around every
  handler, and what a program checks there is its own, which is why
  [`core-classes/ratelimit-two-members`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ratelimit-two-members) declines to decide what a limit does for a route.
- **`HEAD`-implies-`GET`, an automatic `OPTIONS`, trailing-slash normalisation.** Each is somebody's
  wrong default. The server decides them above the table, visibly
  ([`http-server/head-runs-as-get`](http-server.md#http-server-head-runs-as-get), [`http-server/a-preflight-is-answered-before-any-code-runs`](http-server.md#http-server-a-preflight-is-answered-before-any-code-runs),
  [`http-server/a-trailing-slash-is-never-normalised`](http-server.md#http-server-a-trailing-slash-is-never-normalised)).

<sub>See also [`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked), [`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered), [`core-classes/router-signed-url`](core-classes.md#core-classes-router-signed-url), [`core-classes/ratelimit-two-members`](core-classes.md#core-classes-ratelimit-two-members), [`types/grammar`](types.md#types-grammar), [`security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`](security.md#security-access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning), [`routing/matched-once-before-the-handler`](routing.md#routing-matched-once-before-the-handler), [`routing/a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path`](routing.md#routing-a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path), [`routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`](routing.md#routing-a-match-is-not-invocable).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-match-is-not-invocable"></a>

## A match carries its row and typed parameters and nothing invocable, and typed `callable` would not change that  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`

`Core\Router\Match` carries the matched row, which `is` compares a method reference against, the
typed captures the path filled, the declared verb and the access decision's name, and nothing
invocable: no `->invoke()`, no callable, no class-and-method
strings, and the handler's `Class::method` label never crosses. A first-class reference to the
matched method would need `callable` to carry a signature, which [`types/grammar`](types.md#types-grammar) defers — but
routing is not a forcing case for that deferral, and a typed `callable` on the match would not be the
way to dispatch, for three independent reasons.

What a match returns beyond its captures, and why:

- **`is(Shop::show)` returns whether that method's route matched.** It takes a method reference and
  returns a `bool`, so it identifies a route the way a link names one without handing anything
  invocable back. A written reference folds to the row index while compiling; a reference passed as
  a value is compared by row when the call runs.

- **`access()` returns the decision's name**, such as `App\Role::Admin`, never the constant's value.
  The compiler checks that the name resolves and promises nothing about what it means, so the name is
  the one thing the row carries without interpreting it. `null` comes only from a table built by hand,
  because a route with no decision does not compile, and a dispatcher treats `null` as denied.
- **`method()` returns the verb the matched row declares.** Two `#[Route]`s on one method share
  its path, and `is` is `true` for both, so only the verb tells a `Get` match from a `Post` match.
- **The handler's `Class::method` label stays off the match**, because it is the one field of the row
  a program could turn into a call.
- **`attribute<T>()` returns the matched method's attribute payload of the shape `T`**, folded while
  compiling and looked up by the label on the runtime's side, so the label still does not cross
  ([`routing/a-match-reads-an-attribute-as-data`](routing.md#routing-a-match-reads-an-attribute-as-data)).
- **Memory:** each read of `Core\Request::route()` or `Core\Router::match` holds one string, the length
  of the decision's name, and two integers, the verb and the row's place in the table. A program that
  never reads a match pays nothing.

Routes do not share a signature: `show(uint $id)`, `index()` and `blog(uint $y, uint $m, string $slug)`
cannot inhabit one `handler` field, and pre-binding the converted parameters into a zero-argument callable
is dispatch. Handlers have no common return type, and a `callable(): Response` would force one, which is
a framework opinion `Core` refuses to hold. And a callable on the match would be a second way to reach a
handler, around the gate `Core\Router::dispatch` puts in front of every one
([`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler)). That call is generated code in the unit, indexed
by the matched row, so dispatching needs nothing from the match a program could call. The roster of
compiler-recognised attributes this table draws on has one home
([`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute)), and no rule restates its size.

**Declined:**
- **The server calls the matched method.** The program calls `dispatch`, and a program that does not
  is served as before ([`routing/the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing`](routing.md#routing-the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing)).
- **`params` as a shape per route, narrowed by `is`.** The checker has no such narrowing,
  and it would save only one `as`. The generated jump binds typed parameters without it.

<sub>See also [`routing/the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing`](routing.md#routing-the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing), [`types/grammar`](types.md#types-grammar), [`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler), [`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute), [`routing/matching-is-not-dispatching`](routing.md#routing-matching-is-not-dispatching).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-match-reads-an-attribute-as-data"></a>

## `Core\Router\Match::attribute<T>()` returns the one attribute payload on the matched route's method that satisfies the shape `T`, folded while compiling  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/a-match-reads-an-attribute-as-data`

`$match->attribute<T>()` returns the one attribute payload on the matched route's method that satisfies
the shape `T`, or `null` where none does. It is the payload `Core\Attributes::get<T>(Class::method)`
returns for that method ([`attributes/structural-retrieval`](attributes.md#attributes-structural-retrieval)), so a gate reads a per-route option such
as `#[{seconds: 60}]` with `$route->attribute<{seconds: int}>()` and keeps no table of routes of its
own.

The payload is data folded while compiling ([`attributes/retrieval-folds-while-checking`](attributes.md#attributes-retrieval-folds-while-checking)). At each
call site the compiler folds `T` once for every method that carries a `#[Route]`, and the call is handed
those payloads keyed by each method's `Class::method` label. The matched row's label is read on the
runtime's side and the entry under it is returned, so the label never becomes a value the program holds
and the payload, a shape of constants, has nothing on it to call ([`routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`](routing.md#routing-a-match-is-not-invocable)).
A routed method with no payload of the shape has no entry, and the call returns `null` for it.

The refusals are the retrieval's own, reported at the call:

- **`T` that is not a shape** is `E0729`. A payload matches by its fields, so only a shape can select one.
- **Two payloads of the shape on one routed method** is `E0728`, naming that `Class::method`. Any route
  may be the one that matched, so every routed method is held to the one-match rule `get<T>` holds its
  target to.
- **A matching payload with a value that has no constant form** is `E0731`, as it is for `get<T>`.

- **Memory:** each match holds one more integer, its row's place in the table. Each call builds one
  array and one payload object per routed method that matches `T`, and frees all of them but the one
  it returns when it returns. A program that never calls `attribute` pays the integer only.

**Declined:**
- **Options keyed by a route's path.** One method may serve two routes, and a route is identified
  by its method, so the method is what carries an option.
- **Returning the handler label, so a program looks the payload up itself.** The label is the one field
  of a row a program could turn into a call ([`routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`](routing.md#routing-a-match-is-not-invocable)).
- **A reflection table read at run time.** Retrieval has an answer before the program starts, and a
  compiled unit carries no reflection table ([`attributes/retrieval-folds-while-checking`](attributes.md#attributes-retrieval-folds-while-checking)).

<sub>See also [`routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`](routing.md#routing-a-match-is-not-invocable), [`attributes/structural-retrieval`](attributes.md#attributes-structural-retrieval), [`attributes/retrieval-folds-while-checking`](attributes.md#attributes-retrieval-folds-while-checking), [`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler).</sub>

<a id="routing-matched-once-before-the-handler"></a>

## A request is matched once, before any application code runs, and `Core\Request::route()` is that match  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/matched-once-before-the-handler`

The server matches the incoming request against the compiled table **once**, before any application
code runs, and records the result on the request. `Core\Request::route(): ?Core\Router\Match` returns
that match. `null` means the table claimed nothing for this method and path — or the program declared no
`#[Route]` at all, which builds no table and matches nothing. Nothing during the request can move it:
the match lives on the request carrier rather than on the context, so there is no place a second match
could be written from inside the program.

It is what three readers were written against. The CSRF check ([`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default))
needs to know which handler a `POST` is for, the `route` metric label needs the route's path pattern, and the
access decision rides on it uninterpreted ([`security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`](security.md#security-access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning)).
Each reads the door's answer rather than matching again, which **removes** a match for most requests
rather than adding one — a match is about a quarter of the header parse the server performs anyway.

`Core\Router::match(Http\Method, tainted string)` remains for matching some *other* verb and path the
caller chose. It takes the same walk as the door, so the two cannot disagree about one path, and an
in-process test request ([`testing/in-process-request`](testing.md#testing-in-process-request)) crosses the door's match the same way.

The one program that pays for the door's match and reads nothing from it has a route table, has
metrics off, serves a safe verb and never reads its own route. Every route carries an access decision
([`attributes/access-is-a-required-sibling`](attributes.md#attributes-access-is-a-required-sibling)) that a dispatcher reads off the match, so that
program is close to an empty set.

**Declined:**
- **Leaving the match to the application.** Most requests would be matched twice, once for the CSRF
  check or the `route` label and once by the program, and the two matches could disagree about one
  request.

<sub>See also [`routing/the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing`](routing.md#routing-the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing), [`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default), [`security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`](security.md#security-access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning), [`testing/in-process-request`](testing.md#testing-in-process-request), [`routing/matching-is-not-dispatching`](routing.md#routing-matching-is-not-dispatching), [`routing/table-is-opt-in`](routing.md#routing-table-is-opt-in).</sub>

<a id="routing-the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing"></a>

## The server's match dispatches nothing, and a request the table does not claim is served by the program

`rule:routing/the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing`

The server computes a name and typed parameters and stops there. It never calls the annotated method,
never decides what a return value means, and never wraps anything: the route table is complete without
crossing into dispatch. The program calls the handler, through `Core\Router::dispatch`
([`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler)) or a `switch` of its own, and a program that does
neither is served exactly the same way.

So a request the table does not claim is an ordinary served request. `route()` answers `null`, the
program runs exactly as it would for any other request, and the `404` — if it is one — is something the
program sends, not something the door refuses with: `dispatch` sends it through the gate's `refused`.
A door that refused a miss would refuse every request of a program declaring no `#[Route]`, which is the
opt-in table inverted.

The boundary holds one layer down as well. `Core\Router::match` answers a `Core\Router\Match` and
nothing invocable ([`routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`](routing.md#routing-a-match-is-not-invocable)), and the one decision the server enforces on
a match is CSRF ([`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default)) — the access name rides through for whoever
dispatches to read. A request the door refused still runs a program that calls `dispatch`, in refusal
mode, where `route()` answers `null` so no handler is reachable and only the gate answers.

<sub>See also [`routing/matched-once-before-the-handler`](routing.md#routing-matched-once-before-the-handler), [`routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`](routing.md#routing-a-match-is-not-invocable), [`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default), [`routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`](routing.md#routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler), [`routing/matching-is-not-dispatching`](routing.md#routing-matching-is-not-dispatching), [`routing/table-is-opt-in`](routing.md#routing-table-is-opt-in).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path"></a>

## A missing path and a refused verb are different answers, and `methodsFor` is what tells them apart

`rule:routing/a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path`

`Core\Router::methodsFor(tainted string $path): array<Http\Method>` tells a missing path from a refused
verb. An empty array means no route claims the path at all — `404`. A non-empty one means the path
exists under other verbs — `405`, and the list is the `Allow:` header RFC 9110 requires beside it. Each
verb appears once, as a `Core\Http\Method` case, in declaration order.

It is asked only after `Core\Request::route()` or `match` has answered `null`, so a served request pays
nothing for it, and `match` keeps its two-state return rather than growing a verb list on the success
path where nobody reads it. A program with no `#[Route]` answers the empty array, because "no route
claims this path" is exactly true of it.

Where an optional trailing capture makes a node terminal
([`routing/a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent`](routing.md#routing-a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent)), both forms report the same verbs:
`methodsFor("/posts")` on a table declaring `/posts/{page?}` returns that route's verbs, so the shorter
form cannot `404` while the longer one `405`s. A plain `OPTIONS` is answerable by an application from
this list; the server still answers none on its behalf, because which to answer is a convention.

**Declined:**
- **A third state on `match`'s return.** Beside the verb list nobody reads on success, every caller
  would destructure three cases to use one.
- **A `404` for a refused verb.** It breaks RFC 9110, and it hides nothing: a `GET` to the path
  already shows that the path exists.

<sub>See also [`routing/matched-once-before-the-handler`](routing.md#routing-matched-once-before-the-handler), [`routing/a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent`](routing.md#routing-a-trailing-segment-may-be-absent), [`routing/matching-is-not-dispatching`](routing.md#routing-matching-is-not-dispatching).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-gate-answers-around-every-handler"></a>

## `Core\Router::dispatch` calls the matched method, and one gate answers every request it refuses or that fails

`rule:routing/a-gate-answers-around-every-handler`

`Core\Router::dispatch(Core\Router\Gate $gate): void` calls the method of the route the server matched,
and the gate the program passes answers every request that method does not run for.

```nvs
interface Core\Router\Gate {
    public function allows(Core\Router\Match $route): bool;
    public function refused(Core\Router\Refusal $reason, ?Core\Router\Match $route): void;
    public function failed(?Core\Router\Match $route, ?Throwable $error): void;
}

interface Core\Router\Responder extends Core\Router\Gate {
    public function respond(Core\Router\Match $route, mixed $value): void;
}
```

The compiler generates the jump from the route table it already builds, one entry per route, indexed
by the matched row, so no program writes or keeps a list of its routes. The jump is code in the unit
and never a value: the handler's `Class::method` label still does not cross into the program, and the
match stays not invocable ([`routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`](routing.md#routing-a-match-is-not-invocable)). **A handler may declare any return
type, and a returned value reaches the response only through the program's own `respond`.** When the
handler's declared return type is neither `void` nor `never` and the gate implements
`Core\Router\Responder`, `dispatch` calls `$gate->respond($route, $value)` once the handler returns,
then releases the value; a `?T` handler that returns `null` still reaches `respond` with `null`. The
gate writes the response, as `Core\Response::html` does for a `Core\Html\Markup`. A plain gate drops
the value, and so does a gate that declares a `respond` method without implementing `Responder`: the
name alone never decides it. A handler that throws reaches `failed` and never `respond`, a refused
request reaches neither the handler nor `respond`, and an error `respond` throws is thrown by
`dispatch`. Either way the declared type is what `nvs build --openapi` describes as the response body
([`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table)). **`nvs check` warns at a `dispatch`
whose gate cannot be a `Responder` while a handler returns a value** (`W1025`), at the gate argument,
naming up to three such handlers in load order and then how many more. "Cannot be" is over every
non-abstract class the program declares: the argument's static type must admit none that implements
`Responder`, and a type naming no class of the program, such as `Core\Router\Gate` or `mixed`, admits
all of them. So the warning is never wrong about the program as written, and a program with a
`Responder` that passes a plain gate through a wide type gets none. It is never an error: a program
that wants the value dropped writes a `respond` that does nothing, or declares the handler `void`.
A handler is a static method or a
method of a class with a no-argument constructor; any other `#[Route]` method is a compile error at its
attribute, because the jump has no arguments to build an instance with.

**`allows` runs before every handler, and the handler runs only when it returns `true`.** A `false` or
a throw is `Refusal::Denied`. This is the dispatch site that reads `#[Access]` on every route
([`security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`](security.md#security-access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning)): a route cannot reach its handler around
it, because the jump is the only call to the handler `dispatch` makes.

**`refused` answers what the table or the server refused, and never overturns it.** `dispatch` sets
the status before it calls `refused`, so a gate that only renders a page sends the right code, and the
gate may set another status, headers, the body and a log line. The handler never runs. The cases of
`Core\Router\Refusal`:

| Case | Status | When |
|---|---|---|
| `NotFound` | `404` | no route claims the path |
| `MethodNotAllowed` | `405`, with `Allow` from `Core\Router::methodsFor` | the path exists under other verbs ([`routing/a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path`](routing.md#routing-a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path)) |
| `UnknownMethod` | `501` | the verb is none of `Core\Http\Method`'s cases |
| `Denied` | `403` | `allows` returned `false` or threw |
| `Csrf` | `403` | the server refused the request's CSRF token or origin ([`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default)) |
| `BodyTooLarge` | `413` | the body is over the cap the server enforces, or a handler read a body over `[limits] request_body` and then threw |
| `BadCapture` | `400` | a capture whose type implements `Parses` threw from `parse` |

A server refusal added later is a new case. A body read that stops at `[limits] request_body` throws
`RuntimeError` and is recorded on the request, so a handler that throws after it reaches `refused`
with `BodyTooLarge`: the size is the client's fault, and a handler that caught only `ParseError`
would otherwise answer it `500`. A handler that catches the throw and returns answers as it chose.
**`failed` answers every other handler that threw,** and a program
stopped by its memory or CPU-time limit: that one runs again in a fresh isolate under the same limits,
with no body, and `failed` is told no route and no error, because the first run's isolate is gone and
a limit is not a throw. If the second run fails too, the answer is the empty `500` a failing program
has always sent, and nothing runs a third time. `dispatch` sets `500` before it calls `failed`.

**Refusal mode is how the server's own refusals reach the gate.** The door decides exactly as it does
for any program. For a request it refused for CSRF, for its body size or for an unknown verb, it then
runs the entry anyway: `Core\Request::route()` returns `null`, so neither `dispatch` nor a dispatcher a
program wrote can reach a handler; the request has no body; and `dispatch` reads the refusal off the
request and calls `refused`. A gate that throws there leaves the empty answer the door would have sent.
The door chooses the mount before it checks the verb, which moves nothing else because a mount is
chosen by path, and the in-process door does the same, so `Core\Test::request` exercises it.

**Only a program that calls `Core\Router::dispatch` gets refusal mode.** The compiler sees the call, as
it sees a link ([`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked)), and marks the unit. A program that
dispatches by hand keeps the empty answers, because it would read a refused request as an ordinary one
with no route. `Core\Request::route()` and `Core\Router::match` serve it unchanged.

Some refusals never reach a gate. A CORS preflight's body is never shown by a browser
([`http-server/a-preflight-is-answered-before-any-code-runs`](http-server.md#http-server-a-preflight-is-answered-before-any-code-runs)). Malformed HTTP has no request yet,
and an unreadable `X-Forwarded-For` is read by a proxy. A socket that is also an event stream has
already ended. The capacity and drain `503`s and a path no mount covers are answered where no code may
run, so their pages, when they exist, are static and come from the configuration.

- **Memory:** one generated jump entry per route, per program. Nothing per request beyond the isolate
  the request already has; a refused request that reaches the gate costs what any request costs. A
  dispatching program's request keeps its head until its run ends, which the door held anyway, and
  a run a limit stopped pays for one more isolate under the same ceiling. `respond` adds one bit per
  route row and one per class descriptor, per compiled unit, and nothing per request.
- **Latency:** `respond` is one more method call, only for a request whose handler returns a value and
  whose gate is a `Responder`. A `void` handler or a plain gate pays one bit test.
- **Usability and simplicity:** a page is a method that returns its markup, and a test calls it as one,
  for one more interface and one warning. Security is unchanged, because `allows` still runs before
  the handler. The warning costs the checker one walk over the program's classes per `dispatch` call.

**Declined:**
- **A dispatch `switch` every program writes.** It repeats every `#[Route]`, nothing checks it, and an
  arm that forgets a route serves nothing while one that forgets `accessAs` serves the route unguarded.
- **A gate that can overturn a refusal.** A refusal would then depend on code a reviewer has to read
  beside the route. The one opt-out from CSRF stays `csrf: false` on the route itself.
- **The server calling the matched method.** The program calls `dispatch`, and a program that does not
  call it is served exactly as before ([`routing/the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing`](routing.md#routing-the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing)).
- **Refusal mode for every program.** A hand-written dispatcher would read a refused request as an
  ordinary request with no route.
- **A built-in return-value-to-response rule.** Which value becomes which response is a framework
  opinion, so `dispatch` hands the value to the program's own `respond` and decides nothing about it.
- **Constructor injection.** It is a framework opinion, and a handler built by a no-argument
  constructor needs none.
- **Every handler returns `void`.** The OpenAPI document reads a route's response schema and its
  `#[Api]` example from the return type, so the rule would remove both from every document.

<sub>See also [`routing/matching-is-not-dispatching`](routing.md#routing-matching-is-not-dispatching), [`routing/a-match-is-not-invocable`](routing.md#routing-a-match-is-not-invocable), [`routing/the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing`](routing.md#routing-the-servers-match-dispatches-nothing), [`routing/a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path`](routing.md#routing-a-refused-verb-is-not-a-missing-path), [`security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`](security.md#security-access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning), [`security/csrf-is-on-by-default`](security.md#security-csrf-is-on-by-default), [`testing/in-process-request`](testing.md#testing-in-process-request).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-request-reads-its-mount"></a>

## `Core\Request::mount()` answers the prefix the door stripped and the tainted host captures, and it is never `null`

`rule:routing/a-request-reads-its-mount`

`Core\Request::mount(): Core\Request\Mount` answers the two facts about the door a request came through:
`prefix(): string` is what the mount stripped from the path before the program saw it, and
`captures(): array<tainted string>` are the mount's glob captures in order — `{1}` is `captures[0]`.
The captures are `tainted` because they came off the wire ([`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier)), so
feeding one to a query launders normally; the prefix is the deployment's own plain text. One member for
the pair, because a request holding one mount's prefix and another's captures is a bug the shape rules
out.

**`mount()` is never `null`**, where `route()` is. A request the table does not claim is an ordinary
served request, but every request that reached a program reached it *through* a mount, and a door that
strips nothing answers `""` and an empty array rather than an absence. With no request at all it
refuses, like every other reader of the class ([`security/request-state-throws-in-an-isolate`](security.md#security-request-state-throws-in-an-isolate)).

This is how one compiled table serves many tenants, and why `#[Route]` gains no `host` field: a path is
source state and a hostname is deployment state, so each lives where it changes, and the table stays
relocatable to `/ModuleA`, `/ModuleB` or `/` with no recompile. A program never derives its own prefix
from the request target.

<sub>See also [`routing/matched-once-before-the-handler`](routing.md#routing-matched-once-before-the-handler), [`routing/an-origin-is-per-mount-and-checked-at-boot`](routing.md#routing-an-origin-is-per-mount-and-checked-at-boot), [`security/tainted-qualifier`](security.md#security-tainted-qualifier), [`security/request-state-throws-in-an-isolate`](security.md#security-request-state-throws-in-an-isolate), [`routing/link-carries-the-mount-prefix`](routing.md#routing-link-carries-the-mount-prefix).</sub>

<a id="routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked"></a>

## `Core\Router::url` is a launderer that takes its route as a method reference, and a reference and `$params` written in the code are checked against the compiled table  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`

`Core\Router::url(callable $route, array<string, mixed> $params = []): string` takes the route by its
method reference — `Router::url(App::show, ['id' => 3])` — and reverses the table from that method.
The compiler resolves the call against the whole program's table after every file has been walked, so
the route may be declared in a file the scan reaches later.

**A reference written at the call is checked while compiling**, and each failure is an error reported
at the argument: **a method that does not exist**, **a method with no `#[Route]`**, and **a `$params`
array literal that does not cover the route's captures** — every `{name}` and `{name...}` the path
writes needs a key of that name, and only a `{name?}` may be left out, whose whole segment is then
dropped. A key in that array literal that is neither a capture nor one of the route's declared
`#[Query]` parameters is refused in the same shape, so a typo cannot silently become a query
parameter. `$params` defaults to `[]`, so a route with no captures is linked as `Router::url(App::home)`.

**A reference passed as a value**, such as a menu entry built elsewhere, is resolved when the call
runs, and the call throws when the method has no route. A computed `$params` is not checked at all —
there are no keys to read.

**A link calls nothing**, so an instance method needs no object (`App::show` names it whether or not
it is `static`), and its visibility is not checked: a `private` handler is linked to like a `public`
one.

**A literal value is held to the conversion of the parameter it supplies**, a capture's or a
`#[Query]` parameter's, and one the conversion refuses is `E0772` at the call: `"x"`, `-3` and `2.5`
for a `uint`. The check runs the matcher's own conversion on the segment the value builds, for the
types the matcher converts itself (`int`, `uint`, `decimal`, `Core\Uuid`); a closed set is
[`routing/a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set`](routing.md#routing-a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set)'s. A `float` literal is refused for each of those but
`decimal` without being turned into text. A computed value, a `string` parameter and a class built from
text are not checked, so a link is a path its route matches wherever the value is written at the call.

The result is a laundered URL path ([`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named)): each substituted
value is percent-encoded into its own segment under RFC 3986's component rules, so a `tainted`
parameter produces a plain `string` that is safe *as a path* and for nothing else. `urlAbsolute` is
the same link with a configured origin in front, and refuses exactly the same targets. The path a link
is built on is the mount-relative one ([`routing/link-carries-the-mount-prefix`](routing.md#routing-link-carries-the-mount-prefix)).

**Declined:**
- **Checking the handler's visibility.** A link builds a path and invokes nothing, so a `private`
  handler is no less reachable for being linked to; the route's `#[Access]` is what guards it.

<sub>See also [`routing/route-attribute`](routing.md#routing-route-attribute), [`routing/link-carries-the-mount-prefix`](routing.md#routing-link-carries-the-mount-prefix), [`routing/path-grammar`](routing.md#routing-path-grammar), [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named), [`routing/an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin`](routing.md#routing-an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin), [`routing/a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string`](routing.md#routing-a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string), [`routing/a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture`](routing.md#routing-a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture).</sub>

<a id="routing-link-carries-the-mount-prefix"></a>

## A link carries the mount prefix the request arrived under, so one table serves at any mount  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/link-carries-the-mount-prefix`

`Core\Router::url` prepends the prefix of the mount the request arrived through, in front of the
substituted path. One compiled table then serves the same module at `/ModuleA`, at `/ModuleB` or at
`/` with no recompile — a path is source state and a mount is deployment state, so the prefix is
known only where the request is — and it is why link generation goes through this member rather than
concatenating a declared path: a link assembled from the declaration is wrong the day the module is
mounted anywhere but the root.

A program run off the command line is mounted nowhere and the prefix is empty; nothing else about the
link changes ([`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked)). `urlAbsolute`'s configured origin
is the other half of an absolute link, and is read from the resolved unit rather than from any header.

The prefix is read off the request the door already wrote it on
([`routing/a-request-reads-its-mount`](routing.md#routing-a-request-reads-its-mount)), never derived from the request target, and all three of
`url`, `urlAbsolute` and `urlSigned` join it — a signed link survives a remount because what is
signed is the route's path pattern and its parameters, never the mounted URL. A test describes its door with
`Core\Test::request`'s `mount` key, so what a mounted deployment writes is pinned without a server.

<sub>See also [`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked), [`routing/a-request-reads-its-mount`](routing.md#routing-a-request-reads-its-mount).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string"></a>

## A `url()` key that is not a capture becomes a percent-encoded query string, and one that is neither a capture nor a declared `#[Query]` parameter does not compile  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string`

A `$params` key handed to `Core\Router::url` or `urlAbsolute` that names no capture becomes a
percent-encoded query string, spelled exactly as `Core\Uri::buildQuery` spells it:
`url("posts.index", {page: 3, sort: "desc"})` on `/posts/{page?}` folds to `/posts/3?sort=desc`. The
link is still the launderer's ([`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named)) — a paginated link has a
laundered spelling, where `url(…) . "?page=" . $n` is the concatenation the launderer exists to prevent
and re-taints the result.

The refusal half is the same sentence. A key written in the `$params` array literal that is neither a capture nor one of the route's
declared `#[Query]` parameters ([`routing/a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture`](routing.md#routing-a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture)) is a
**compile error**, in the same shape as the missing-route and missing-capture errors, so a typo cannot
silently ship as a query parameter. The declared type says what a query *value* arrives at; it does not
constrain what a link may be handed, except that a literal outside a closed set is refused
([`routing/a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set`](routing.md#routing-a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set)).

**Declined:**
- **Refusing every key that is not a capture.** A link with a query string would have no laundered
  spelling, and every paginated link would fall back to concatenation.

<sub>See also [`routing/a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture`](routing.md#routing-a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture), [`routing/an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin`](routing.md#routing-an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin), [`routing/a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set`](routing.md#routing-a-capture-narrows-to-a-closed-set), [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named), [`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked).</sub>

<a id="routing-an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin"></a>

## `urlAbsolute` prepends a configured origin and never one sniffed from a request header  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin`

`Core\Router::urlAbsolute(callable $route, array<string, mixed> $params = []): string` is `Core\Router::url`
with the configured origin in front — the same laundered path, the same query-string rule
([`routing/a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string`](routing.md#routing-a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string)), the same compile errors for a method with no
route or an uncovered capture — joined with exactly one `/` whatever the origin's trailing slash.

**The origin is configuration, never inference.** It is resolved before the program runs, out of
`[[app]] origin`, and is never derived from `Host` or `X-Forwarded-Host`: deriving an origin from a
header is host-header injection, and an emailed password-reset link is where it lands. A unit that
resolves no origin throws from `urlAbsolute` rather than answering a link with an empty authority in it —
`url` still answers for the same route, because a path needs no origin.

The two members are two names on purpose. One `url()` whose absoluteness depended on configuration would
mean two different things at one call site depending on a file the reader is not looking at, and would
break the property that one compiled table serves at any mount prefix. Where the origin comes from when
one binary serves several hosts is [`routing/an-origin-is-per-mount-and-checked-at-boot`](routing.md#routing-an-origin-is-per-mount-and-checked-at-boot).

<sub>See also [`routing/a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string`](routing.md#routing-a-leftover-link-key-is-a-query-string), [`routing/an-origin-is-per-mount-and-checked-at-boot`](routing.md#routing-an-origin-is-per-mount-and-checked-at-boot), [`security/launderers-are-sink-named`](security.md#security-launderers-are-sink-named), [`routing/link-target-and-params-are-checked`](routing.md#routing-link-target-and-params-are-checked).</sub>

<a id="routing-an-origin-is-per-mount-and-checked-at-boot"></a>

## An origin is declared per mount with `[app] origin` as the fallback, a request cannot set it, and a mount that calls `urlAbsolute` without one is a boot error

`rule:routing/an-origin-is-per-mount-and-checked-at-boot`

The origin `urlAbsolute` prepends ([`routing/an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin`](routing.md#routing-an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin)) is
declared **per mount**, on the `[[server.mount]]` block, falling back to `[app] origin`. A single global
origin is wrong for a host-mounted deployment the server already supports: one binary serving
`tenant1.example.com` and `tenant2.example.com` would put one tenant's origin in the other's email. The
same `{1}` that selects the mount builds its origin — `origin = "https://{1}.example.com"` — so onboarding
a tenant is zero new configuration, and the request reads the same captures back through
[`routing/a-request-reads-its-mount`](routing.md#routing-a-request-reads-its-mount).

`origin` is `System`-class: a request may not set it, because a value a request can choose is a value an
attacker can influence, and this one ends up in mail. It is `Reload`-able, so a new tenant needs no
restart. **The check that an origin resolves runs at mount expansion**, per resolved mount, and re-runs
on reload: a mount whose unit contains a literal `urlAbsolute` call and resolves no origin is a boot
error, so the failure is at deploy time rather than in a sent message.

**The check is asked at the boot compile**, which is the first point at which both halves are in hand:
`nvs serve` compiles every mounted entry before it binds anything, and asks of each resolved row whether
the unit it just compiled builds an absolute link. One entry serves every tenant a `scan` glob
enumerated, so the same unit is a refusal under a row that resolved no origin and a start under the row
beside it. A served request then receives its mount's origin on the isolate that answers it, because a
process serving many mounts has no one origin its accept loop could hold. A reload that changes a
`[[server.mount]]` block expands the table again ([`http-server/a-mount-table-expands-at-boot`](http-server.md#http-server-a-mount-table-expands-at-boot)),
and a reload that moves `[[app]] origin` folds it into the rows again. Either way the same check is
asked of every row that changed, so a row that no longer resolves an origin is left out of the table
and the reason is logged.

**Declined:**
- **An origin a request may set.** The `tainted` qualifier stops a header copied straight in, but not
  a value laundered through a database round trip, and this value ends up in mail.
