<sub>See also [`routing/an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin`](routing.md#routing-an-absolute-link-takes-a-configured-origin), [`routing/a-request-reads-its-mount`](routing.md#routing-a-request-reads-its-mount), [`http-server/the-server-block-is-boot-class`](http-server.md#http-server-the-server-block-is-boot-class).</sub>

<a id="routing-table-is-opt-in"></a>

## The table is built by the program enumeration, and a program with no `#[Route]` builds none and pays nothing  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/table-is-opt-in`

Finding routes is the question the program enumeration was built for — *what exists that nothing
names* — and the route table is that enumeration filtered by `#[Route]`, reused wholesale with its
consequences ([`programs/implementing`](programs.md#programs-implementing)):

- **A program containing no call to a member whose answer comes from the table performs no scan of
  the autoload roots**, the identical opt-in rule a discovery query has, and any one of them alone
  opts it in. Those members are `Core\Request::route()` and `Core\Router`'s `dispatch`, `match`,
  `methodsFor`, `url`, `urlAbsolute`, `urlSigned` and `signedRoute`. `route()`, `signedRoute` and
  `dispatch` read the match the door took, and that match is taken against the table, so without the
  scan a front controller reading `route()` over autoloaded routes would get `null` on every request,
  and an entry whose only call is `dispatch` would compile none of the classes it dispatches to. `Core\Request::mount()`
  reads the mount table and does not opt in. A program with no `#[Route]` anywhere pays nothing,
  including no pass. A running program with no table matches nothing and serves the request however
  it likes. The table still holds every `#[Route]` of every class the program compiles, each one
  linkable by its method, so the door's CSRF check covers every handler that can run, scan or no scan.
- **The scan makes the compiled unit depend on directory contents**, so every listed directory joins
  the revalidation set: no new dependency kind and no new directive. Zero under `validate = never`,
  which is what production runs.
- Routes in files reached by an ordinary `require` are included too; they are already in the graph.
  Rows accumulate across every file into one program-wide table, which is where a duplicate between
  two files is caught ([`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered)).

The table is a compile product carried by the unit and installed before the program runs, beside the
command table and the configuration snapshot; the match against it is taken once at the door, and
the door dispatches nothing ([`routing/matching-is-not-dispatching`](routing.md#routing-matching-is-not-dispatching)). A link to a route declared in another
module needs that module compiled — the consequence [`programs/no-runtime-autoload`](programs.md#programs-no-runtime-autoload) already
records for a hard cross-module reference, arriving in a second place.

- **Memory:** the table costs O(routes in compiled code) in the artifact, not per request and not
  per object. A program with no `#[Route]` holds none.

<sub>See also [`programs/implementing`](programs.md#programs-implementing), [`programs/no-runtime-autoload`](programs.md#programs-no-runtime-autoload), [`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered), [`routing/matching-is-not-dispatching`](routing.md#routing-matching-is-not-dispatching), [`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table).</sub>

<a id="routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table"></a>

## The API document is generated from the route table while compiling, so it cannot drift from the code  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`

The OpenAPI 3.1 document is a rendering of the compiler's own route table. Every fact in it was
decided by the front end and is read off a row; the emitter parses, resolves and infers nothing.
A specification generated from the code cannot disagree with the code, which is the failure every
hand-written or annotation-scanned API document eventually has.

What supplies what: the path and verb come from `#[Route]`'s `path` and `method`; the `operationId`
is the handler's `Class.method`, with the lowercased verb as a suffix when the method serves several
verbs ([`routing/a-method-is-one-endpoint-everywhere`](routing.md#routing-a-method-is-one-endpoint-everywhere)), and `#[Api]`'s optional `operationId`
replaces it for a public API whose clients must keep their function names. A method rename changes
the derived `operationId`, and [`routing/api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change`](routing.md#routing-api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change) reports it as
breaking, which is its job. Path parameters from the handler's own parameters, by declared type, which is the binding matching
already makes; query parameters from `#[Query]` parameters, a default making one optional; the
response body from the declared return type, a class in it being a `components.schemas` entry of
its JSON codec's fields ([`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute)) and an enum its backing values, which
is what that codec writes; required-ness from definite initialization and
parameter defaults, decided rather than guessed; nullability from `?T` and nothing else; an
enumeration from a closed enum's cases or a set of allowed values; the summary and description from
the declaration's doc comment — first sentence, then the rest. What the types cannot say comes
from `#[Api]` ([`attributes/api-adds-and-cannot-contradict`](attributes.md#attributes-api-adds-and-cannot-contradict)), which may add and may not
contradict.

**A path is written as an OpenAPI path template, and the document is valid 3.1.** A `{name...}` is
written `{name}`, because 3.1 has no rest template. A path parameter is always required in 3.1, so a
route with a `{name?}` is two paths: one with `{name}` required, and one that ends before that
segment, whose `operationId` takes a `.without-<name>` suffix. A test holds every fixture's document
to the official 3.1 schema and its Schema Object dialect, and checks that every `$ref`, `security`
name, `operationId` and template name resolves.

**A program with no `#[Route]` generates nothing and runs no pass**, and a program the front end
refuses emits no document at all rather than a partial one. A handler returning `mixed` produces a
useless schema, visibly, which is the correct incentive.

The document is only as precise as the handlers' types, and the type system is what makes it precise:
every variable has a declared type, a property is definitely initialized, `?T` is the only
nullability, and an enum is closed, so each maps onto JSON Schema without guessing. A doc comment is
already parsed for tooling, so reading it adds no machinery, but it makes the comment part of a
published artifact.

**Declined:**
- **Reflecting over the route table at run time**, the way annotation-scanning frameworks build their
  document. It is compile-time work done at run time, it needs a cache that goes stale, and it cannot
  make a contradiction a compile error, which is the whole value
  ([`attributes/api-adds-and-cannot-contradict`](attributes.md#attributes-api-adds-and-cannot-contradict)).
- **A hand-written specification the compiler checks the code against.** It makes the document a
  second source of truth kept in sync in the other direction, and a check strong enough to be worth it
  is a much larger feature. Nothing stops a team from diffing a generated document against a
  hand-written one with [`routing/api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change`](routing.md#routing-api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change).
- **Generating clients.** The OpenAPI generator ecosystem exists and is specialised per target
  language, so Novis emits the input it reads rather than reimplementing it.
- **GraphQL and gRPC descriptions.** The document is OpenAPI alone; a handler that does not answer JSON
  is an operation with an opaque response
  ([`routing/api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact)).

<sub>See also [`routing/api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact), [`routing/api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change`](routing.md#routing-api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change), [`routing/a-method-is-one-endpoint-everywhere`](routing.md#routing-a-method-is-one-endpoint-everywhere), [`attributes/api-adds-and-cannot-contradict`](attributes.md#attributes-api-adds-and-cannot-contradict), [`core-classes/derive-attribute`](core-classes.md#core-classes-derive-attribute), [`security/route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type`](security.md#security-route-capture-is-laundered-by-its-type), [`routing/a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture`](routing.md#routing-a-query-parameter-is-declared-like-a-capture).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-request-body-is-read-from-the-handlers-own-call"></a>

## A route's request body is the type its handler decodes with `Core\Request::jsonAs` or `postAs`, read from the handler's own call

`rule:routing/a-request-body-is-read-from-the-handlers-own-call`

The compiler records each `Core\Request::jsonAs<T>()` and `Core\Request::postAs<T>()` call written
directly in a route handler's body, and the route's row carries what it found: the body is `T`, as JSON
for `jsonAs` and as a form for `postAs`. The API document writes it as the operation's `requestBody`,
with `T`'s schema under `application/json` or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
([`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table)). A JSON body is `required`, because
`jsonAs` throws on an empty body. A form body is `required` when `T` has a required field, because
`postAs` throws when one is missing.

There is no new syntax. The type is the one the handler already writes to decode its body, so the
document cannot name a body the code does not decode ([`attributes/api-adds-and-cannot-contradict`](attributes.md#attributes-api-adds-and-cannot-contradict)).
A handler with a `jsonAs` and a `postAs` gets both media types. Two reads of one kind with different
types give that media type a `oneOf` of the two schemas. A `postAs` call that writes its `name` option reads
one field of the form and not the whole body, so the document does not take a body from it.

A body read inside a helper method is not seen. A handler that reaches a `jsonAs` or `postAs` call only
through methods it calls gets no `requestBody`, and `nvs check` warns at the route that the document does
not describe its body (`W1027`). The warning follows the calls the checker resolved, through any number of
methods, and does not follow a call through a `callable` or a `mixed` receiver. Moving the read into the
handler removes the warning.

- **Memory:** one body entry per route row, on the compile path only. The checker keeps one list of
  resolved callees for each method that calls one, until every route is in. The warning's walk then
  visits each method once per route that reads no body itself. Nothing runs per request.

**Declined:**
- **An `#[Api(body: ...)]` field.** It could name a type the handler does not decode, the contradiction
  [`attributes/api-adds-and-cannot-contradict`](attributes.md#attributes-api-adds-and-cannot-contradict) forbids.
- **A body parameter the server decodes before the handler runs.** It is new syntax and a second way to
  read a body.
- **Following a helper's body read into the document.** The published API would then change when a read
  moves between two methods, without any change to the handler.

<sub>See also [`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table), [`attributes/api-adds-and-cannot-contradict`](attributes.md#attributes-api-adds-and-cannot-contradict), [`routing/route-attribute`](routing.md#routing-route-attribute).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-security-scheme-is-declared-in-code"></a>

## A security scheme is declared in code by `#[Api\Scheme]`, and every `#[Api]` `security` name must be a declared one  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/a-security-scheme-is-declared-in-code`

A security scheme is declared in the program, by a compiler-recognized `#[Api\Scheme]` on a class,
and every name an `#[Api(security: [...])]` writes must be one the program declares.

```nvs
use Core\Api\KeyIn;
use Core\Api\Scheme;
use Core\Api\SchemeType;

#[Scheme(name: "bearer", type: SchemeType::Http, scheme: "bearer", format: "JWT")]
#[Scheme(name: "key", type: SchemeType::ApiKey, in: KeyIn::Header, parameter: "X-Api-Key")]
class Auth { … }

#[Route(path: "/orders/{id}", method: Method::Get)]
#[Access(allow: Role::User)]
#[Api(security: ["bearer"])]
public static function show(uint $id): Order { … }
```

The attribute is repeatable and may sit on any class. A qualified name is absolute
([`statements/a-qualified-name-is-absolute`](statements.md#statements-a-qualified-name-is-absolute)), so a file writes it `#[Core\Api\Scheme]` or imports
it with `use Core\Api\Scheme;`, and `use Core\Api;` alone does not place it. Its fields are OpenAPI 3.1's Security Scheme
Object, spelled the way `#[Api]` spells its own fields. The scheme names form one program-wide set,
because `components.securitySchemes` is one map per document.

| `type` | Required | Optional | Written to the document as |
|---|---|---|---|
| every type | `name: string`, `type: Core\Api\SchemeType` | `description: string` | the key, `type`, `description` |
| `ApiKey` | `in: Core\Api\KeyIn`, `parameter: string` | | `in`, `name` |
| `Http` | `scheme: string` | `format: string` | `scheme`, `bearerFormat` |
| `MutualTls` | | | |
| `OAuth2` | `flows` | | `flows` |
| `OpenIdConnect` | `url: string` | | `openIdConnectUrl` |

`type` is an enum, never a string ([`core-api/no-mode-strings`](core-api.md#core-api-no-mode-strings)): `Core\Api\SchemeType` has the five
cases the specification lists. `in` is the enum `Core\Api\KeyIn` for the same reason, with `Query`,
`Header` and `Cookie`. `parameter` is the header, query or cookie name, because `name` is the scheme's
own key. `scheme` stays a string: it is a name from IANA's open HTTP authentication registry, such as
`bearer` or `basic`, and an enum would close a list the specification leaves open.

`flows` is an anonymous object with at least one of `implicit`, `password`, `clientCredentials` and
`authorizationCode`. Each flow is an anonymous object with `scopes`, an array from scope name to its
description (`[]` for none), and the URLs its kind needs: `authorizationUrl` for `implicit`, `tokenUrl`
for `password` and `clientCredentials`, both for `authorizationCode`. `refreshUrl` is optional on each.

**The compiler checks both ends.** A `security` entry naming no declared scheme does not compile, and
the message lists the names the program declares, so a typo is a compile error rather than a document
that references nothing (`E0886`). Two declarations of one name do not compile, and the error names
both sites (`E0887`). A field the scheme's `type` does not take, a required field left out, and a flow
that is not one of the four or lacks its URL are errors where they are written (`E0888`). A field no
type takes is the ordinary unknown option. A declared scheme that no route names is not an error: a
document may describe a scheme before a route uses it.

**The route table carries the declared schemes**, and `nvs build --openapi` writes them to
`components.securitySchemes`, sorted by name, so the document stays deterministic
([`routing/api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact)). The emitter still reads every fact
off the table ([`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table)). A program that declares
no scheme writes no `components.securitySchemes`.

A scheme describes; it enforces nothing. Who may call a route is `#[Access]`'s decision
([`attributes/access-is-a-required-sibling`](attributes.md#attributes-access-is-a-required-sibling)), and a request runs the same with or without an
`#[Api\Scheme]` in the program.

- **Memory:** nothing per request. While compiling, one row per declared scheme and one entry per
  written `security` name, held in the route table.

**Declined:**
- **Schemes in `nvs.toml`.** The compiler never reads a deployment's configuration, so it could not
  check a `security` name against it, and the document would depend on which file a build saw.
- **A guessed definition for an undeclared name.** The emitter would be stating a fact about
  deployment that nobody wrote ([`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table)).
- **Checking that `#[Access]` and the scheme agree.** An access decision is a name the compiler does
  not interpret ([`security/access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning`](security.md#security-access-is-checked-for-presence-not-meaning)), so there is nothing to
  compare it with.
- **`type` and `in` as strings, as the specification spells them.** A mode string is a typo the
  compiler cannot see ([`core-api/no-mode-strings`](core-api.md#core-api-no-mode-strings)), and the document still writes the
  specification's spelling.
- **Scopes as an anonymous object.** A scope name such as `orders:read` is not a field name a
  program can write, so the scopes are an array keyed by string.

<sub>See also [`attributes/api-adds-and-cannot-contradict`](attributes.md#attributes-api-adds-and-cannot-contradict), [`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table), [`routing/api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact), [`attributes/access-is-a-required-sibling`](attributes.md#attributes-access-is-a-required-sibling).</sub>

<a id="routing-api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact"></a>

## `nvs build --openapi` writes OpenAPI 3.1 as a build artifact, and two builds of one source are byte-identical

`rule:routing/api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact`

`nvs build --openapi <file>` runs the program through the same front end `nvs check` uses and
writes the OpenAPI 3.1 document, pretty-printed, to standard output. It is a build artifact and
never a runtime feature: the running server does not construct it, nothing sits on the request
path for a value that changes only when the code does, and serving it is the first-party
framework's job over a file the build produced.

**Two builds of the same source produce byte-identical documents.** The emitter has exactly two
orderings — paths by their written text, operations within a path by lowercased verb — and both are
sorted rather than left to a map, because [`routing/api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change`](routing.md#routing-api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change) compares
documents and a document that reorders itself between builds makes every diff useless.

OpenAPI 3.1 only, whose schema dialect is JSON Schema, so every declared type maps without loss. No
3.0 downgrade path and no Swagger 2: an older version would mean deciding what to drop when the
type system says something it cannot express. A handler answering HTML or a stream appears as an
operation with an opaque response — honest, and not very useful.

**Declined:**
- **A document the running server builds and serves as an endpoint.** It puts work on the request
  path for a value that changes only when the code does, which is what the artifact cache is for.

<sub>See also [`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table), [`routing/api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change`](routing.md#routing-api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change).</sub>

<a id="routing-api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change"></a>

## `nvs api diff` classifies every change as breaking, additive or cosmetic, and exits non-zero on a breaking one

`rule:routing/api-diff-fails-a-breaking-change`

`nvs api diff <old.json> <new.json>` compares two generated documents as JSON values rather than as
text, prints one line per change worst-first, and exits non-zero if any change is **breaking**.
Breaking is the ordinary API-compatibility reading: a removed operation, a removed or newly
required parameter or property, a narrowed type, a removed enum case, a removed status code, a
tightened constraint. **Additive** is a new operation, a new optional parameter or property, a new
enum case, a widened type. **Cosmetic** is everything else — a title, a version, a summary, an
`operationId`, a tag.

The classification is mechanical, derived from schemas the compiler produced, not a reviewer's
judgement, and it errs towards breaking: a removed parameter is breaking whether or not it was
optional, and a changed `format` is breaking because the two schemas accept different strings.
**There is no suppression mechanism** — a gate with an escape hatch is advisory, and if one proves
necessary it is an additive change later.

A document that cannot be read or is not JSON is a failure naming the file, never an empty diff:
"nothing changed" and "could not tell" may not share an exit code in a gate. Put the command in CI
against the last release's document and a broken client turns from an incident into a red pipeline.

<sub>See also [`routing/api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-a-deterministic-build-artifact), [`routing/api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table`](routing.md#routing-api-document-is-generated-from-the-route-table).</sub>

<a id="routing-a-quick-fix-writes-a-derived-path"></a>

## A `#[Route]` missing its `path` gets a quick fix that offers a derived one, and nothing derives a path on its own  *(designed — owned by goal routes-by-method)*

`rule:routing/a-quick-fix-writes-a-derived-path`

Nothing derives a `path` from the declaring class. The compiler checks every *internal*
reference to a route and exactly zero *external* ones, so a derivation rule would turn a class
rename into a silent move of the URL that is
in a bookmark, an email, another service's configuration and a search index. A path is a public
interface; a class name is an implementation detail.

What survives of convention routing is the typing, and a quick fix buys it without the coupling: on
the `E0747` diagnostic for a `#[Route]` whose required `path` is missing, the editor offers the
derived path as replacement text the developer accepts, edits or ignores. The derivation is fixed so
two machines produce one string:

- the declaring class's **short name**, a trailing `Controller` removed, `PascalCase` to kebab-case
  ([`core-api/identifier-casing`](core-api.md#core-api-identifier-casing));
- then the method's name, `camelCase` to kebab-case, **omitted entirely for `index`**;
- then one `{name}` segment per parameter carrying no `#[Query]` whose declared type is a capture
  type, in declaration order — a `Request` or a service contributes nothing.

So `UserController::show(uint $id)` offers `/user/{id}`, `UserController::index()` offers `/user`,
and `AdminUserController::listPending(Request $r)` offers `/admin-user/list-pending`. **Nothing is
pluralized**: pluralization is English-only and irregular, and editing the inserted text is the
point of inserting text rather than deriving a path.

This is a fix, not a generator. A generator's output has to be *right*
([`ide/a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined`](ide.md#ide-a-code-action-writes-only-what-is-already-determined)), and a URL is not
type-determined by anything; this output is a starting point, read as a diff before it is accepted.
The fix is backed by a diagnostic the checker already emits, since `path` is a required field of
`Core\Route` ([`ide/a-quick-fix-is-a-diagnostics-own-suggestion`](ide.md#ide-a-quick-fix-is-a-diagnostics-own-suggestion)).

**Built:** no path is derived, and `E0747` reports a `#[Route]` with no `path`
(`crates/nvs-types/src/routes.rs`, `crates/nvs-types/tests/routes.rs`). Its suggestion writes `path:
"…"` before the payload's first field, or as the whole payload where there is none (`derived_path` in
`crates/nvs-types/src/routes.rs`), and
`tests/lsp/actions/a-route-with-no-path-is-offered-the-derived-one.lspt` freezes the edit. The fix is
not safe, since the URL it writes is a starting point.

**Declined:**
- **Convention routing**, a `path` the compiler derives from the class and method. It makes a
  route free to declare, and is pleasant where the URLs are nobody's API, but it welds a public interface
  to an implementation detail. A quick fix writes the derived path once instead, and that path is real
  text: searchable, and stable under every later rename.

<sub>See also [`routing/routes-are-compiled-not-registered`](routing.md#routing-routes-are-compiled-not-registered), [`core-api/identifier-casing`](core-api.md#core-api-identifier-casing), [`routing/route-attribute`](routing.md#routing-route-attribute).</sub>
